# SK1042 — The nested `if` statements can be combined

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An `if` whose entire body is another `if` with no `else` is one condition written as two.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Syntax |
| Needs a compilation | no |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S1066 |

## Why

The second `if` adds a level of nesting and no branch: there is no path where the outer condition holds and the inner one does not lead anywhere else. `&&` short-circuits, so the merged form evaluates exactly what the nested one did, in the same order — and it stops the nesting counting against the `SK7006` depth metric for a structure that never had two branches.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
if (order != null) {
    if (order.IsPaid) {
        Ship(order);
    }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
if (order != null && order.IsPaid) {
    Ship(order);
}
```

## When it does not fire

A whole chain is one finding reported at its top, so the fix never overlaps another and the rule is silent after its own fix. Any `else` anywhere in the chain excludes it, as does an outer body holding anything besides the inner `if`. An operand that `&&` would capture — `||`, `??`, a conditional or an assignment — is parenthesised rather than merged flat. Names a merged condition introduces (a pattern variable, an `out var`) have their scope widened by the rewrite, so the whole member is scanned for a colliding declaration first and the finding is dropped if one exists; the scan deliberately over-bails, counting names that could never conflict. Comments and preprocessor directives anywhere outside the surviving body exclude the chain, and so does a `#` inside a condition's string literal.
